title: Defense Exports Hit Record $5.79B, Kurdish Peace Bill Clears Committee, Fidan Says Mecca Pact Matches NATO Article 5
subhead: Turkish defense exports surged 26.2% year-on-year to $5.79B in the first seven months of 2026, while the Kurdish peace bill passed the Justice Committee and FM Fidan declared the Mecca defense pact equivalent to NATO's Article 5 — with Egypt potentially joining.

sections.heading: Kurdish Peace Bill Clears Justice Committee
sections.body:
Turkey's Parliamentary Justice Committee approved the 'Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Unity Act' on Saturday, advancing the PKK disarmament framework to the full parliamentary agenda. The 12-article bill establishes a legal mechanism tied to the dissolution of the PKK and KCK, with security institutions verifying the end of armed activity and the National Security Council (MGK) confirming compliance (Kurdistan24, The Hindu).

Justice Minister Akın Gürlek denied reports that imprisoned former HDP co-chair Selahattin Demirtaş would be excluded, according to TGRT News, which contacted Gürlek directly after journalist Abdulkadir Selvi reported that both Demirtaş and PKK leader Abdullah Öcalan would be ineligible. Gürlek's denial leaves open the possibility that Demirtaş could benefit depending on the final text (Kurdistan24).

The bill proposes deferring investigations and sentences for eligible cases — five years for sentences under 15 years, 10 years for longer sentences — with permanent closure if no new crimes occur. Exclusions include those convicted of intentional murder and those sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment before June 1, 2005. Oversight would involve a senior council chaired by the vice president and a 17-member parliamentary monitoring committee (Kurdistan24, Al-Monitor).
sections.whyItMatters: Committee passage moves the bill to the general assembly floor, the first formal legislative step since the PKK announced its dissolution. The Demirtaş question remains unresolved and politically explosive — his inclusion or exclusion could determine whether the process commands Kurdish buy-in.

sections.heading: Fidan: Mecca Pact Is 'Technically' NATO Article 5, Egypt Could Join
sections.body:
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told Anadolu Agency that the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed Friday by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan is 'technically the same as NATO's Article 5' mutual defense clause. He emphasized the pact does not target Iran or any country unless a member state is attacked, and that allies would decide through consultations the 'degree, form, and format' of support (Reuters/AOL, AP).

Fidan said President Erdogan wants the alliance to expand beyond three members, identifying Egypt as a potential candidate once 'certain technical matters are resolved.' The four nations — Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Egypt — had held multiple rounds of consultations (dubbed 'R4') over the past year focused on regional security and the US-Iran conflict (Reuters/AOL).

However, Egypt did not sign the pact despite participating in preparatory talks. Alhurra reports that Cairo has not issued an official explanation, and no evidence exists that Egypt was formally invited and declined. Analyst Gamal Raif told MBN that Egypt's constitution limits overseas military deployments, requiring National Defence Council consultation and a two-thirds parliamentary majority for combat missions. Egypt also maintains diplomatic channels with Iran (Alhurra).

A general secretariat will be based in Saudi Arabia, with operational details to be set at the first ministerial committee meeting. Fidan said the pact had been under negotiation for two years and eight months (Reuters/AOL).
sections.whyItMatters: Fidan's Article 5 comparison raises the stakes — it signals Ankara views this as more than a symbolic gesture. Egypt's absence is the key gap: without Cairo, the pact covers the Gulf but not the Eastern Mediterranean or North Africa.

sections.heading: Defense Exports Hit Record $5.79B in Seven Months
sections.body:
Turkish defense exports reached $5.79 billion in the first seven months of 2026, up 26.2% year-on-year, according to Al-Monitor citing Defense Industry Agency data. July alone accounted for $1.12 billion, a 14.4% increase over the same month last year. The 12-month rolling total now stands at $11.2 billion (Al-Monitor).

The surge reflects sustained demand for Turkish drones, armored vehicles, and naval platforms across the Gulf, Central Asia, and Africa — markets where Turkey has built production and training partnerships alongside its weapons sales.
sections.whyItMatters: The export trajectory validates Turkey's defense-industrial strategy and gives Ankara hard-currency leverage in its foreign policy relationships. The $11.2B rolling annual figure puts the 2026 full-year target of $10B+ well within reach.

sections.heading: Syria's Shibani Visits Ankara, Condemns Israeli Strikes
sections.body:
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani met with Fidan in Ankara, where both sides agreed to establish a High-Level Strategic Council between Turkey and Syria. Shibani updated Turkish officials on Kurdish integration efforts and condemned Israeli attacks on southern Syria (Al-Monitor).

The visit continues the rapid normalization track between Ankara and the new Damascus administration, formalizing institutional ties that would have been unthinkable under the Assad government.
sections.whyItMatters: The Strategic Council framework locks in Turkey's post-Assad influence in Damascus. Shibani's decision to condemn Israel from Ankara — not from an Arab League platform — signals where Syria's new government sees its primary patron.

sections.heading: Digital Lira Enters Phase 3 Live Sandbox
sections.body:
Turkey's central bank advanced 23 private-sector projects from 85 applicants into the Phase 3 live sandbox for the digital lira CBDC, according to MSN. The sandbox will test five categories: programmable payments, tokenized deposits, machine-to-machine transactions, cross-border interoperability, and offline payments.

The Phase 3 step moves the digital lira beyond theoretical modeling into controlled real-environment testing with actual financial institutions — a significant milestone for the project that has been running since 2021.
sections.whyItMatters: The digital lira sandbox puts Turkey ahead of most G20 economies in CBDC development. Programmable payments and tokenized deposits, if successful, could reshape how Turkish banks intermediate capital and how the state disburses social transfers.

sections.heading: Bulgaria Investigates Drone Blast Near Turkey-Ukraine Gas Pipeline
sections.body:
A drone entered Bulgarian airspace and exploded near a major gas pipeline linking Turkey and Ukraine, close to Bulgaria's border with Romania. Bulgarian authorities launched an investigation and increased security measures. No casualties were reported (MSN).

The incident raises questions about whether the strike was aimed at energy infrastructure transiting the region — and about the vulnerability of overland gas corridors running through the Balkans.
sections.whyItMatters: If confirmed as a deliberate targeting of the Turkey-Ukraine pipeline, this would extend the scope of the Russia-Ukraine conflict into EU and NATO territory — Bulgaria — and threaten the energy transit routes Turkey has been building as alternatives to maritime routes.

sections.heading: Economy: Inflation Eases to 31.75% in July
sections.body:
Turkey's annual consumer price inflation edged down to 31.75% in July from 32.11% in June, according to TurkStat data reported by Daily Sabah and confirmed by MSN. The Central Bank's policy rate stands at 37%, slightly above inflation — a real rate that remains positive but barely (Bianet, Daily Sabah).

Over three years of Mehmet Şimşek's economic program, inflation has fallen only 6.46 percentage points from its peak, a pace that has frustrated businesses and households alike. The lira continues to face pressure from the regional conflict's impact on energy import costs (Bianet).
sections.whyItMatters: Inflation is decelerating but not collapsing. With real rates barely positive and regional energy costs elevated, the Central Bank has little room to ease — keeping Turkey in a slow-grind stabilization that strains political patience.

bottomLine: Saturday was a day of milestones: the Kurdish peace bill cleared its first legislative hurdle in committee, defense exports hit a record pace, and Fidan framed the Mecca pact as NATO-equivalent — with Egypt potentially next. But Egypt's absence from the signing tells its own story, and the digital lira sandbox quietly advanced a project that could reshape Turkish finance more than any defense deal.
sources: Al-Monitor, The Hindu, Kurdistan24, Reuters/AOL, AP, Alhurra, MSN, Daily Sabah, Bianet, Aviation Week, AEI, India TV News, Shillong Times, RFE/RL
